*Theory and Research Note, November 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author's own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated.*


Research note to accompany the proposal *Sovereign Incentives for Decarbonisation: How Multilateral Development Banks Can Use Financial De-risking to Lower the Cost of Capital and Reward Climate Policy*. Written 1 November 2026. Public sources only: no World Bank internal material is used.

**Status.** Draft for Stephen's review, not for submission. Sources come from web searches run on 1 November 2026, many of them trade press, advocacy or policy summaries. Every figure marked `[VERIFY]` must be checked against the primary source before use. Names marked "memory" were not checked in any source. Links are inline; the full annotated bibliography is in `AnnotatedBibliography-FinancingAndIncentives.qmd`.

# 1. Summary and overall research question

Net-zero infrastructure in emerging and developing economies (EMDEs) is mainly a financing problem, and the financing problem is mainly about who guarantees the payment. Solar, wind, grids and electric transport are almost all upfront cost, so what investors charge for capital sets what the service costs. Investors charge less when a creditworthy party stands behind a long-term payment. Every structure reviewed here, from power purchase agreements (PPAs) to regulated asset bases to management contracts, is a way of packaging that guaranteed payment. Each depends on a government's credibility, which is the sovereign's own choice.

The proposal already asks how multilateral development banks (MDBs) can lower the cost of capital for clean power while making early decarbonisation the sovereign's preferred choice. This addendum widens the frame from power generation to the whole system (networks, vehicles, public investment). It adds the currency tools a guarantee needs, the standard metrics for cost and risk, and the fiscal and growth case a finance ministry cares about. It suggests this overall research question, with the proposal's three questions kept as sub-questions:

> **When a government's payment obligation is guaranteed, finance follows. Which guaranteed-payment structures, backed by which balance sheet and in which currency, deliver net-zero infrastructure at the lowest cost to the sovereign and to the guarantor, and how should the price of that guarantee depend on the sovereign's own policy credibility?**

The question is deliberately narrower than "how do we finance net zero". It names one mechanism, the guaranteed payment, and one design variable, the link between its price and policy credibility.

# 2. Sovereign incentives

Carbon markets create sovereign incentives, but in the wrong direction. A host government that sells credits under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement must subtract the sold reductions from its own national count (a "corresponding adjustment"). The more ambitious its target, the costlier each sale, so a government earns more by keeping its target weak. The [World Bank's paper on corresponding adjustments](https://ppp.worldbank.org/public-private-partnership/sites/default/files/2023-10/Corresponding%20Adjustment%20and%20Pricing%20of%20Mitigation%20Outcomes.pdf) says the more ambitious the host's national target, the higher the cost of the adjustment. A [*Climate Policy* article (2022)](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/14693062.2022.2108366) argues that baselines tied to national targets give hosts a motive to set weaker targets. A [second article (2021)](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14693062.2021.1948384) argues that crediting outside the national target, without adjustments, can give hosts perverse incentives not to extend their policies. The industry body IETA also treats the adjustment as [a sovereign risk](https://www.spglobal.com/energy/en/news-research/latest-news/energy-transition/060622-carbon-market-players-face-significant-sovereign-risk-from-article-6-activities-ieta), while Verra and the integrity council ICVCM [dispute that ambition will freeze](https://www.spglobal.com/energy/en/news-research/latest-news/energy-transition/060823-corresponding-adjustments-should-not-be-enforced-in-voluntary-market-verra-icvcm). Evidence on the size of the effect is thin: one preprint says the link between voluntary market transactions and national target delivery is largely unquantified `[VERIFY: preprint status]`. Cullenward and Victor's [*Making Climate Policy Work*](https://www.lowyinstitute.org/publications/david-victor-how-make-climate-policy-work) (2020) gives the wider critique that carbon markets are layered on regulation and are politically captured; only secondary summaries were read.

The common fixes work on credit accounting. Corresponding adjustments and ambition-linked baselines stop credits being double counted. None of them pays a government for setting a stronger target.

Finance can pay for ambition directly, and the practice is small. The World Bank's [report on results-based climate finance](https://www.tcafwb.org/sites/default/files/2023-05/WB_RBCF_Report_FINAL.pdf) covers paying governments for predefined climate results. The [2023 joint MDB report](https://thedocs.worldbank.org/en/doc/3077331569469f690c6e82b35052766c-0020012024/original/2023-Joint-Report-on-MDB-Climate-Finance.pdf) shows results-based financing of roughly $4.3 billion against $10.7 billion for policy-based financing `[VERIFY]`. I found no study of guarantees or credit enhancement priced on credible national climate policy. That is the gap the proposal fills, but the finding comes from searches that do not prove nobody has written on it. Searching Google Scholar for "conditional guarantee", "policy-contingent" and "ambition-linked", and asking Nadia Ameli and Michael Grubb, should come before any claim of novelty.

Grubb has made a related argument for Norway's balance sheet. His Financial Times opinion piece of 24 August 2023, ["Norway has a chance to transform climate finance"](https://www.ft.com/content/c4bf95e2-6868-448d-bfca-5871dd2fb492), says on its standfirst that Norway's windfall from the energy crisis should be used to underwrite investments in developing countries. Only the headline, standfirst and date reached this note; the body of the article was not read, so its mechanism and numbers are unchecked `[VERIFY: read the full article]`. The standfirst is enough to show the link to the thesis: a rich-country sovereign balance sheet is proposed as the guarantor of developing-country investment.

Jayant Sinha's ORF issue brief, ["A Green Bank for Global South Climate Finance"](https://www.orfonline.org/research/a-green-bank-for-global-south-climate-finance) (Issue Brief 678, 7 December 2023), builds the same idea into an institution. It proposes a private-sector-oriented Global Green Bank, capitalised with a few billion dollars of equity from sponsoring countries, sovereign funds and philanthropies, plus hard callable capital to earn an AAA or AA rating. It names Norway, Canada, Saudi Arabia and the UAE as possible sponsors and cites a figure of $138 billion of 2022 fossil-fuel windfall gains for Norway alone `[VERIFY: figure in the brief]`. The bank would sit in the Global South, take on country and climate risk through blended finance, use existing guarantee programmes and act as a market maker for long-term currency hedging. The brief makes claims on cost of capital but does not model them (section 3). It is a proposal from a single author, and it does not link the bank's terms to the borrowing country's policy, which is the variable the thesis adds.

The link to the proposal's model is direct. The government adopts a package when S + F(Δr) − λL ≥ O, where F(Δr) is the financing saving from a lower cost of capital. Carbon-market crediting acts on the left side of that inequality in the wrong direction, because it lowers the payoff to a stronger target. A policy-priced guarantee raises F(Δr) for governments that keep their commitments. The two can be compared on the same formula.

# 3. De-risking, including currency

De-risking works by narrowing the gap between a project's cost of capital and the sovereign's, and it rarely closes it. The proposal cites an IEA estimate that a typical solar plant in EMDEs faced a cost of capital two to three times that in advanced economies and China in 2021 `[VERIFY: IEA Cost of Capital Observatory]`. Private project finance seldom beats its own sovereign. Brazil's transmission auctions show this: bidders compete hard (a [commercial source](https://energy-solutions.co/policy-intelligence/permitting-and-red-tape/brazil-transmission-auctions-aneel) reports discounts of 40 to 50% below the regulator's revenue cap `[VERIFY]`), yet the [IEA's Brazil case study](https://www.iea.org/reports/brazil-case-study/grids-in-brazil-mobilising-private-capital-through-a-robust-regulatory-framework) says the regulator builds its allowed return from US Treasury yields plus Brazil's emerging-market bond spread, which sits above Brazil's own cost of borrowing. The savings in these auctions come from competition and efficiency, not from cheaper money.

Guarantees and credit enhancement are the standard tools for narrowing the gap. An [Asian Development Bank paper](https://www.adb.org/sites/default/files/publication/468626/ewp-564-risk-mitigation-sovereign-guarantees-ppps.pdf) estimates that an MDB partial risk guarantee cuts the cost of debt by about 125 basis points `[VERIFY: scenario]`, and the saving varies with whether the sovereign counter-indemnifies the guarantee. MDB experience suggests the risk premium exceeds realised losses: pooled default and recovery data show a 94.9% average recovery on sovereign and sovereign-guaranteed loans over 1984 to 2023 (GEMs Consortium, 2024, cited in the proposal), and [Zero Carbon Analytics](https://zerocarbon-analytics.org/finance/capital-expenditure-solar-wind-emerging-markets-could-reach-356-billion-2040/) reports a 2.61% average default rate on MDB and development-finance loans to private borrowers in 159 countries `[VERIFY]`. The [IISD guide](https://www.iisd.org/system/files/2026-08/guide-guarantees-sovereign-debtors.pdf) adds that guarantees can lengthen maturities and lower interest rates but cannot compensate indefinitely for macroeconomic problems. For electric two- and three-wheelers, [UNEP's Capital 2 Mobilize work](https://www.unep.org/en/events/online-event/capital-2-mobilize-financing-electric-two-and-three-wheeler-transition-global) finds that financing-cost differences mostly reflect macroeconomic and customer risk, not a premium for the technology, and that EV-specific de-risking achieves little in very high-cost markets such as Nigeria and Brazil `[VERIFY]`.

**Currency belongs in the de-risking box of tricks, because a hard-currency loan to a local-currency earner moves the risk to the borrower.** Renewable projects in developing countries earn revenue in local currency, so foreign-currency debt is risky for them. The [OECD's work on local currency financing](https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2025/02/unlocking-local-currency-financing-in-emerging-markets-and-developing-economies_af15df6a/bc84fde7-en.pdf) notes that the high cost of hedging and of borrowing in these currencies makes MDB local-currency loans unattractive to borrowers, especially sovereigns. The main tools are:

- **Cross-currency swaps and forwards.** The Currency Exchange Fund ([TCX](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/blended-finance-case-studies_2fb90b9a-en/the-currency-exchange-fund_321fe70e-en.html)) provides mainly non-deliverable cross-currency swaps and forwards, so a lender can raise hard currency while the borrower takes local-currency debt. Sources report over $10 billion of local-currency funding across 140-plus currencies by 2024 `[VERIFY]`. Hedges are priced at a spread over the gap between dollar and local-currency interest rates, so a swap converts the currency risk into a known cost and does not remove it.
- **Local-currency PPAs.** TCX's [perspectives paper](https://www.tcxfund.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/TCX-Perspectives-LCY-PPAs-final.pdf) makes the case for PPAs that pay in local currency, and a [*Development Policy Review* article](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/dpr.70096) proposes tenders that bundle a local-currency PPA with optional hedging support.
- **Partial credit guarantees to local banks.** GuarantCo-style guarantees let local banks and institutional investors lend to power producers in local currency for longer terms. The [Climate Policy Initiative](https://www.climatepolicyinitiative.org/publication/managing-currency-risk-to-catalyze-climate-finance/) paper on managing currency risk covers donor-funded options such as hedge-cost subsidies and portfolio risk guarantees.
- **Direct MDB local-currency lending.** The World Bank's section on [addressing exchange rate risk in infrastructure](https://thedocs.worldbank.org/en/doc/0f9533593fd01402ff6f68c0cd74ed28-0360012024/original/Addressing-Exchange-Rate-Risk-in-Infrastructure-Projects-in-EMDEs.pdf) reviews the options.

Sinha's [Global Green Bank brief](https://www.orfonline.org/research/a-green-bank-for-global-south-climate-finance) puts currency at the centre of the case. It says rooftop-solar businesses in India and Africa pay 15 to 18% in local currency, and that long-term currency hedging could be "hundreds of basis points cheaper" than rolling over one-year hedges. A highly rated bank holding capital against losses on currency contracts would make the market. The brief does not model these effects, so the figures are claims, not results `[VERIFY]`.

The limits matter. One analysis argues that hedges of 15 to 20 years, the tenor power projects need, are available from almost no provider at a viable cost ([Energy Transition Africa](https://www.energytransitionafrica.com/insights/article/currency-risk-african-energy-projects-political-risk-mismatch-explained)), and local-currency finance remains a small share of most MDB portfolios. Currency risk is also partly a sovereign risk, because the exchange rate reflects the country's macroeconomic credibility. Avinash Persaud's currency-risk guarantee proposals under the Bridgetown Initiative are relevant here (memory `[VERIFY]`).

Four implications follow for the thesis. First, the benchmark for any project structure is the sovereign's own cost of funds, so the target is the distance to the sovereign, not to an advanced-market rate. Second, the cost to the guarantor is expected loss and capital used, not face value, as the proposal's third quantity already says. Third, in the highest-risk countries de-risking one technology does little, and the sovereign's credibility is the binding constraint. Fourth, currency is a separate risk component that the project-finance model in work package 2 should carry explicitly, with the swap, the local-currency PPA and the guarantee compared on cost per dollar of risk removed.

# 4. Policy and finance framework for investment

A guaranteed payment is the common unit, and the financial structure sits on top of it. Once a creditworthy party stands behind a defined payment stream, lenders and investors can price it, pool it, refinance it and sell it. The question for each asset is which structure creates that payment most simply.

| Asset | Structure | Who bears payment risk | Evidence and caveat |
|---|---|---|---|
| Generation (solar, wind, storage) | Competitive auction of a long-term PPA or contract for difference (CfD) | The utility or government counterparty; a guarantee or payment-security fund backs it | UK CfDs run about 15 years with a top-up when prices fall below the strike price. The [CfD design paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.17508) cites Fabra and Neuhoff for government-issued long-term contracts, because the private market for them lacks liquidity. [Brattle](https://www.brattle.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/10/7487_the_importance_of_long-term_contracting_for_facilitating_renewable_energy_project_development_weiss_sarro_may_7_2013.pdf) finds long contracts cut financing cost. |
| Networks (transmission, distribution) | Regulated asset base (RAB): the regulator sets an allowed return on the assets, collected through customer charges | Customers, under a regulator that must keep its commitments | Used for Thames Tideway, Heathrow and [Sizewell C](https://www.constructionenquirer.com/2021/10/26/new-finance-model-to-spur-next-nuclear-plant-builds/), where charges start during construction and the government estimates a £30 billion saving `[VERIFY]`. [Ofgem has warned](https://utilityweek.co.uk/ofgem-sizewell-c-costs-need-to-be-locked-down-before-construction-begins/?amp=true) that consumers could carry overruns. [Oxera](https://www.oxera.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/The-regulatory-asset-base-and-regulatory-commitment-1.pdf-1.pdf) says it works only if regulators keep to the spirit of their commitments. |
| Interconnectors | Cap and floor: revenue is held between a minimum and a maximum | Consumers, within the band | Ofgem introduced it in 2014, with Nemo Link as the pilot ([handbook](https://www.ofgem.gov.uk/sites/default/files/2024-12/Interconnector_Cap_and_Floor_Regime_Handbook_Updated_Version.pdf)). The third application window was [controversial](https://www.newpower.info/2024/03/ofgem-rejects-cap-and-floor-regime-for-six-of-seven-interconnector-proposals/) `[VERIFY: current status]`. |
| Transmission in EMDEs | Independent transmission project or network concession paid by availability, not volume | The utility or sovereign, which needs a guarantee | The World Bank's [*Linking Up*](https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/794221496411403495/pdf/115521-WP-P152573-PUBLIC-June-6-SUPTAEnglishReportWeb.pdf) is the main public reference. Brazil, India, the Philippines and Chile scaled these; Kenya's [30-year concession with Africa50](https://african.business/2026/02/partner-content/africa50-pioneers-africas-first-privately-financed-power-transmission-model-in-kenya) is reported at about $311 million `[VERIFY: contract]`. Payments are usually in local currency (section 3). |
| Distribution | Management contract (the operator is paid a fee to cut losses and raise collections) or concession | The owner of the utility | [CSEP](https://csep.org/working-paper/international-experience-with-distribution-ownership-options-in-developing-countries/) finds management contracts and concessions in Africa mostly raised collection and cut commercial losses. [Auriol](https://www.tse-fr.eu/sites/default/files/medias/doc/by/auriol/developing.pdf) and [ESMAP](https://www.esmap.org/sites/esmap.org/files/DocumentLibrary/FINAL_Private%20Sector%20in%20T&D_KS0023-15_web.pdf) report mixed results for full privatisation. |
| Any public network or asset | Loan from an MDB to the sovereign or state utility | The sovereign | The simplest and cheapest route, using the sovereign's own credit. Limited by borrowing room and MDB lending ceilings. |
| Electric vehicles | Leasing, pooled funds and first-loss guarantees for fleets; risk-sharing facilities for two-wheeler lenders | The lessor or lender, with a first-loss cover | Interest on electric two- and three-wheelers is about twice that on petrol equivalents ([RMI](https://rmi.org/unlocking-low-cost-lending-for-electric-two-and-three-wheelers/)). Banks fear low resale values for e-buses ([IEA](https://www.iea.org/reports/india-case-study/electric-transportation-in-india-accelerating-the-deployment-of-e-buses)). [BasiGo](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/blended-finance-case-studies_2fb90b9a-en/using-flexible-debt-to-support-capital-intensive-e-mobility-businesses_992472ad-en.html) lets Kenyan and Rwandan operators pay for e-buses from operating cash flow. |

Other structures exist that this round did not check `[VERIFY each]`: toll-operate-transfer and asset recycling (selling operating assets to fund new ones), India's hybrid annuity model for roads, viability gap funding (a capital grant that makes a project bankable), and sale-and-leaseback. All fit the same pattern: a defined payment, a creditworthy party behind it, and a regulator or contract that makes the promise credible.

For low-capacity, low-fiscal-space countries the practical rule is the simplest structure that works. That means standard contract templates, centrally run auctions and a guarantee behind the payment, with MDB lending to the utility or sovereign for public networks and private contracts only where delivery capacity or borrowing room is short. Latin American experience suggests PPP grid deals can work where regulators are credible, and simpler routes remain acceptable elsewhere. In practice, the [World Bank's private participation database](https://ppi.worldbank.org) records $100.7 billion of private investment in infrastructure in 2024, and its [annual report](https://ppi.worldbank.org/content/dam/PPI/documents/PPI-2024-Annual-Report-Interactive.pdf) says renewables dominate energy. Investment in the poorest (IDA) countries fell in 2024.

This links to the proposal's first hypothesis. H1 predicts that the fall in the cost of capital from MDB support is larger where policy already provides long-term contracted revenue through auctions, PPAs or CfDs. The structures above are the ways that contracted revenue gets created, and the policy coding in work package 1 could record which each country uses.

# 5. A growth and fiscal story

The finance ministry's case is that net-zero investment and savings policy are the same problem seen from two sides. Developing countries need long-term capital for energy and transport, and ageing countries need long-dated assets to pay pensions. [ECDPM](https://ecdpm.org/work/unlocking-pension-fund-capital-sdgs-and-climate-emerging-markets) puts the emerging-market funding gap for development and climate goals at about $4.2 trillion a year `[VERIFY: scope and year]`. The IMF's [2025 World Economic Outlook](https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/publications/weo/2025/april/english/ch2.pdf) finds that population ageing raises desired savings and pushes interest rates down, and the [ECB](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/pub/pdf/scpops/ecb.op296~aaf209ffe5.en.pdf) links the same effect to a shortage of safe assets. Savings that cannot find safe, long-dated assets in rich countries could finance infrastructure in developing ones, which was the [OECD's argument](https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2000/04/pensions-savings-and-capital-flows_g1gh1371/9789264181625-en.pdf) about pension funds around 2000. The [OECD's 2011 paper](https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2011/09/the-role-of-pension-funds-in-financing-green-growth-initiatives_g17a2011/5kg58j1lwdjd-en.pdf) on pension funds and green growth is a good starting point.

In practice the flow is small. Twenty European pension funds in an [ODI sample](https://media.odi.org/documents/Working_paper_-_trillions_or_billions-full_text_23.05.pdf) held an average of 8.7% of assets in emerging markets `[VERIFY]`, and the [Climate Policy Initiative](https://www.climatepolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/The-State-of-European-Pension-Funds-Net-Zero-Transition.pdf) finds that even large funds face barriers to investing in them. A guaranteed, inflation-linked payment fits their needs: it is long-dated, rated and predictable. This pairing is an inference, not a finding in the sources. It also faces a counter-argument from memory: Charles Goodhart and Manoj Pradhan argue in *The Great Demographic Reversal* that ageing lowers savings and raises real interest rates `[VERIFY]`. If they are right, capital becomes scarcer and de-risking matters more; if the IMF is right, there is spare capital to channel. The thesis would need to take a position or test both.

The question of who funds the guarantor is where sovereign wealth funds enter. Grubb's Norway article (section 2) proposes using a windfall balance sheet to underwrite developing-country investment. If a rich country's sovereign fund backs the guarantee, the pension and sovereign-fund stories become one: the fund supplies the credit, pension capital buys the paper, and the developing country receives cheaper finance.

The fiscal side limits the story. Public investment in EMDEs and low-income countries ran at about 6 to 7% of GDP in a [2015 IMF paper](https://www.imf.org/external/np/pp/eng/2015/061115.pdf) `[VERIFY: update]`. An [IMF working paper](https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/publications/wp/2024/english/wpiea2024232-print-pdf.pdf) using over 80 assessments estimates average efficiency losses of about 34%, and about 53% in low-income countries `[VERIFY]`. The IMF's [Public Investment Management Assessment](https://www.elibrary.imf.org/view/journals/061/2025/001/article-A001-en.xml) (PIMA) covers 82 countries, 37 of them low-income, and its [climate version](https://cfrr.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/2024-06/9_15_3_Sage%20De%20Clerck.pdf) (C-PIMA, launched 2021, over 40 assessments) looks at institutional design only, with no effectiveness scores. A guaranteed payment is a contingent liability for the sovereign, so a guarantee programme must be sized against what the state can absorb (section 7). For the thesis, the sovereign's gain F(Δr) has to be counted net of the contingent liability the guarantee creates.

# 6. Cost and risk of the energy system to government and economy

To a finance minister, cheap power means low system cost financed at a rate the country can bear, without new fiscal risk. The 2025 data support the first part. [IRENA](https://www.pv-tech.org/solar-pv-lcoe-ticks-marginally-upwards-2025-irena/) reports solar PV at about $44 per megawatt-hour and says [over 90%](https://solarquarter.com/2026/07/03/irena-report-over-90-of-new-renewable-power-added-in-2025-was-cheaper-than-fossil-fuels-saving-usd-480-billion-in-fuel-costs/) of utility-scale renewables commissioned in 2025 beat the cheapest new fossil plant; its solar-plus-storage firm power cost is [$54 to $82](https://www.mercomindia.com/levelized-cost-of-solar-plus-storage-fell-to-54-82-mwh-in-2025-irena) in strong regions. [BloombergNEF's benchmarks](https://pv-magazine-usa.com/2026/02/23/solar-lcoe-to-fall-30-by-2035-says-bloombergnef/) are about $39 for solar, about $40 for onshore wind and about $102 for new combined-cycle gas, a record high; four-hour battery storage fell 27% to $78. [Wood Mackenzie](https://www.woodmac.com/ja/press-releases/four-hour-battery-storage-now-beats-gas-peaking-on-cost-globally/) reports four-hour storage beating gas peaking plants in many markets, with a storage cost well above BloombergNEF's `[VERIFY: definitions]`. [Lazard's US solar range](https://pv-magazine-usa.com/2026/07/13/u-s-solar-lcoe-on-the-rise-lazard-says/) rose to $40 to $98 on tariffs.

These are levelised costs, which leave out grid integration and backup and depend heavily on the cost of capital. The finance-ministry view adds five items: the fuel import bill and foreign exchange exposure (IRENA estimates renewables avoided about $480 billion of fossil fuel costs in 2025), price shocks, debt space, contingent liabilities from PPAs, utility losses and guarantees, and revenue effects for fuel exporters and for governments that tax or subsidise fuel.

Finance ministries now have a shared reference for this role. The Coalition of Finance Ministers for Climate Action's guide, [*Strengthening the Role of Ministries of Finance in Driving Climate Action*](https://www.financeministersforclimate.org/sites/default/files/inline-files/Full%20Report%20-%20Conference%20Draft%20-%20Strengthening%20the%20Role%20of%20MoF%2020230413.pdf) (conference draft of 13 April 2023; final version June 2023), was prepared under Finland and Rwanda with support from the Grantham Research Institute at LSE. According to the [LSE summary](https://www.lse.ac.uk/granthaminstitute/news/new-guide-finds-finance-ministries-can-turn-the-tide-on-climate-crisis), it sets out how ministries can mainstream climate into three core functions (economic strategy, fiscal policy and budget management, and financial policy and oversight) through 15 "transformative actions" and more than 140 country case studies. Four of the actions bear directly on this thesis: fiscal policies that change macroeconomic incentives (6), raising, steering and blending finance at scale (9), sustainable investment strategies (13), and the green transformation of state-owned enterprises, national development banks and sovereign wealth funds (14). The PDF itself returned an access error, so I have read only the summary. I cannot say how the guide treats fiscal risk, guarantees, currency or the cost of capital `[VERIFY: read the full guide]`. If it does not treat them in depth, that is a gap the thesis addresses.

Researchers who model costs and technology change include Doyne Farmer, Rupert Way and Penny Mealy at Oxford, Jesse Jenkins at Princeton, and the integrated assessment teams at the Potsdam Institute (Gunnar Luderer) and PBL (Detlef van Vuuren) (memory `[VERIFY]`). On finance and macroeconomics: Ameli, Schmidt, Shrimali, Caldecott, Volz, Persaud, Stern, Bhattacharya, Songwe, Ian Parry, Jean Pisani-Ferry, Patrick Bolton and Kevin Gallagher (memory). I found no author who joins system cost modelling with sovereign balance sheets and incentives. That gap suits the claim to think systemically about risk and finance, and the proposal's link to the Climate Policy Assessment Tool (CPAT) is the bridge, since S and L come from CPAT's sectoral and distributional modules.

# 7. How energy cost, risk and fiscal risk are measured

Standard metrics exist for each of the three, and they map onto the proposal's quantities. The table gives the metric, what it measures and where it comes from.

| Question | Standard metric | What it measures | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| What does energy cost? | Levelised cost of electricity (LCOE) | Cost per megawatt-hour over the plant's life, at a stated cost of capital | [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levelized_cost_of_electricity) (general); IRENA, BNEF above |
| What does it cost the system? | System LCOE, levelised avoided cost of energy (LACE), levelised full system cost | Adds storage and backup for intermittency, or compares cost with the value the plant adds | [CATF, Beyond LCOE](https://cdn.catf.us/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/12134742/beyond-lcoe.pdf); [NREL-based review](https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1768300), which found none of the metrics gives a full view of system cost and value |
| What is the value, not just the cost? | Levelised value of energy, levelised net benefit | Value that cost-only metrics miss | [FTI Consulting](https://www.fticonsulting.com/insights/articles/beyond-cost-metrics-recognizing-value-nuclear-energy) (a consultancy piece; weigh accordingly) |
| How much tail risk does the energy system carry? | Value at risk (VaR) and conditional value at risk (CVaR, the average loss beyond the VaR cut-off) | The loss a plan could suffer at a stated probability; CVaR is the more consistent tail measure | [CVaR planning model for integrated energy systems](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2104.10862) |
| Will the lights stay on? | Loss-of-load expectation, expected unserved energy | Reliability, as the chance or size of a shortfall | [Reliability-focused modelling papers](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.13626) |
| How exposed is the economy to energy prices and imports? | Import dependence, fuel import bill as a share of GDP, price volatility, diversity indices such as the Stirling index | Energy security | Not found in the searches; from memory `[VERIFY]` |
| What is the sovereign's exposure to a guarantee? | Fiscal risk matrix (direct or contingent, explicit or implicit liabilities); stock of guaranteed debt weighted by a probability factor, with a worst-case estimate | The size and likelihood of calls on the budget | IMF [PFRAM 2.0 manual](https://www.imf.org/external/np/fad/publicinvestment/pdf/PFRAM2.pdf) and [2016 guide](https://www.imf.org/external/np/fad/publicinvestment/pdf/PFRAMmanual.pdf); World Bank [fiscal risk toolkit](https://www.worldbank.org/en/programs/debt-toolkit/fiscal-risk) |
| How often do contingent liabilities actually cost money? | Realised fiscal costs | The IMF's [contingent liabilities dataset](https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/wp/2016/wp1614.pdf) finds costs above 20% of GDP rare but the average cost meaningful | IMF WP/16/14 |
| How bad could debt get? | Debt-at-risk: a high percentile of the debt distribution, such as the 95th, some years ahead | Tail risk to the debt path | IMF [Fiscal Monitor, April 2026](https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/publications/fiscal-monitor/2026/april/english/text.pdf) |
| What is the credit risk of a guarantee to the guarantor? | Expected loss (default probability times loss given default times exposure) and capital held against unexpected loss at a high confidence level | The "expected loss and capital used" in the proposal's third quantity | General credit-risk practice, from memory `[VERIFY]`; World Bank [paper on credit risk from government guarantees](https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/977351588579679239/pdf/Assessing-and-Managing-Credit-Risk-from-Contingent-Liabilities-A-Focus-on-Government-Guarantees.pdf) |

So yes, value at risk has a direct role. For the guarantor, expected loss and the capital held against unexpected loss are the credit-risk equivalents of the proposal's "expected loss and capital used". For the sovereign, the IMF's debt-at-risk is a similar tail measure on the whole debt path, and the PFRAM tool turns a guarantee into a fiscal number. For the energy system, CVaR has been used in planning models to cope with price and output uncertainty. The searches found no established "fiscal at risk" or "GDP at risk" metric, so those terms are not used here.

For the thesis this suggests a simple discipline: every structure in section 4 is scored on the same three numbers. The first is its cost of capital (and hence cost per megawatt-hour). The second is its expected loss and capital charge to the guarantor. The third is its contingent liability to the sovereign, on a PFRAM-style basis. Currency adds a fourth item, the cost of the hedge or the unhedged exposure.

# 8. How this fits the proposal

The proposal keeps its three research questions and two hypotheses. This addendum adds an umbrella question (section 1), a longer asset menu, a currency component, a standard metric set and a fiscal cost. The table shows where each piece attaches.

| Addendum idea | Proposal element | What changes |
|---|---|---|
| Carbon markets reward weak targets; Norway as guarantor (section 2) | H2 and the adoption formula | Use the formula to compare crediting with a policy-priced guarantee. Possible validation case. |
| The sovereign is the benchmark; project WACC rarely beats it (section 3) | RQ1 and work package 2 | Report each instrument's cost of capital as a distance to the sovereign's own funding cost. |
| Currency swaps, local-currency PPAs, local-bank guarantees (section 3) | Work package 2 | Add currency as a separate risk component and compare hedge tools by cost per dollar of risk removed. |
| Guaranteed payment as the common unit (section 4) | H1 and work package 1 | Code which structure each country uses (PPA or CfD, RAB, availability payment, management contract, MDB loan). |
| Networks and vehicles, beyond generation (section 4) | Work package 2 and the validation cases | Add one network case, such as an availability-payment transmission concession. Keep scope small. |
| Contingent liability and public investment quality (sections 5 and 7) | The third quantity (MDB cost) and F(Δr) | Add the sovereign's fiscal cost of the obligation as a fourth quantity, net against F(Δr). |
| Ageing, pensions and sovereign wealth (section 5) | Contribution and policy relevance | Frames who funds the guarantee and who buys the paper. Not a new work package. |

A caution on scope. The earlier review of the proposal found that four work packages are too many for three years, and this addendum should not add any. The sensible use is as framing in the introduction and policy sections, one extra case in work package 4, and a policy note after the thesis.

# 9. Appendix: target countries and public investment

**Candidate countries (my judgement, not sourced).** Large emitters: China, India, Indonesia, Brazil, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Mexico, South Africa. Fast-growing: Vietnam, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Egypt, Philippines, Thailand. Low base with large population growth: Nigeria, Ethiopia, DR Congo, Tanzania, Kenya. That makes 20, and the edge choices are arbitrary. The searches found only India (just under 9 Gt of greenhouse gases in 2050 under business as usual, up 95%) and Indonesia (about 3.5 Gt, up 63%) in a [sectoral projections paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43247-024-01288-9) `[VERIFY]`, and that growth in emerging Africa, South-East and Southern Asia and the Middle East will account for most global growth to 2050. A ranking needs country series from the IEA's current-policies scenario or Climate Action Tracker. Nigeria's net-zero target is 2070 and Pakistan's is 2050 (not legally binding); these are targets, not projections.

**Assessing public investment.** PIMA and C-PIMA reports are public for many countries. A first screen for a target country is whether it has one, and what it scores on project appraisal, selection, and the management of state-owned utilities.
